In short, there were all the countless individual unities arising from the joining of possibilities, all the atoms of every universe of existing things. All were present in their entirety and in every aspect: the great and the lowly, the enduring and the perishable, those already gone and those yet to come. They stood there company after company, multitude after multitude, assembled without a single one missing.

passage-en-00312
And all of them turned the face of their very essence toward His Threshold, and fixed the gaze of their existence upon the place of His Presence—yet they did not even know it.

passage-en-00313

All of them spoke through the poverty of their own essence, an essence that possessed no being of its own. All gave voice to the distress of their fleeting selfhood. And all together, in one immense cry of distress and appeal for help, they named Him and invoked Him, implored Him and called upon Him:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00314
“O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! O You who make all things sufficient!”

Yet of this too they were utterly unaware.

Then, amid this appeal that vibrated for the spirit alone, amid this immense hidden clamor, I began to faint. Such was the force of the sadness and bewilderment that overcame me that I almost lost all awareness of my own thinking self. I all but disappeared from the sight of my immaterial soul.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00317
I was on the verge of departing forever from the desert of the Earth of Becoming, of leaving once and for all the shore on which the realm of existence stretches out.

passage-en-00318
But already that fleeting ecstasy was taking its leave of me, leaving nothing behind except longing and tender desire. That lightning-swift rapture abandoned me there, sighing and wounded by sorrow.

And so I returned, once again, to the Earth of ruins and the land of desolation, to the field of falsehood, to the country of illusion...

4. “That Immense Hidden Clamor…”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00320

This extraordinarily beautiful passage from Mîr Dâmâd is remarkable both for the growing intensity of its emotion and for the richness of the language through which he seeks to convey it. The experience was at once visual and auditory. One would need a mystical painter to give form to its symbols, assisted by a musician capable of making them resound.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00321

Yet through the inexhaustible resources of his own language, Mîr Dâmâd manages to communicate something of the image—at once seen and heard—that overwhelmed him to the point of fainting. The successive stages of his ecstatic account closely parallel those in Sohrawardî’s visionary narratives, which themselves express experiences actually undergone. From the very beginning, when the dhikr and the concentration of the mind induce a state of suspension, certain familiar echoes make themselves felt. One is the Avicennian Tale of the Bird, already mentioned in a note.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00322
Another, no less striking, is the ecstasy described by Plotinus, which seems to have served as both model and goal for so many of the spiritual figures we have been studying:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00323
“Often I awaken to myself by escaping from my body. A stranger to everything else, alone in the intimacy of my own being, I behold a beauty beyond all imagining.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00324

This account of ecstasy reached Arabic- and Persian-speaking spiritual thinkers through the Plotinian text known as the Theology of Aristotle. Many, as we know, accepted its attribution to Aristotle without question. Sohrawardî, however, already suspicious of so strange an attribution, openly ascribed the account to Plato. In any case, the Arabic version supplied much of the technical vocabulary that later writers would adopt.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00325

To take just one detail: in the account preserved by the Theology, we read wa-khala'to badanî jâniban; in Mîr Dâmâd’s account, we read fa-ka'annî qad khala'to badanî—“as though I had been stripped of my body.” It is precisely this word, khal', with its suggestion of being unclothed, released, or stripped of the body, that Mîr Dâmâd used in the title of his epistle: Risâlat khal'îya, an Epistle on Being Divested of the Senses, or on being stripped of the bodily condition.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00326

But the comparison cannot be carried through to the end, for the differences soon become apparent. Ashkevarî, the perceptive disciple, had already recognized them. He could hardly avoid mentioning the ecstatic account in the Theology of Aristotle, which he knew so well. He had no wish to diminish its significance.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00327
Yet he suggests quite clearly that the experience of his own master deserves even greater confidence, belief, and acceptance (tasdîq, taslîm, qabûl).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00328

Indeed, he seems anxious to forestall the objections of those who are always ready to doubt for reasons they prefer not to acknowledge—people for whom the spiritual gifts of a contemporary could never possess the authority of events reported to have occurred centuries ago.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00329

But to deny that such experiences can happen again, says Ashkevarî, is to know nothing of the spiritual stages (maqâmât) traversed by those who experience ecstasy. It is to imagine that the One from whom this fullness continually flows is somehow unwilling to give. And our author quotes two lines by Hâfez which, like so many of his verses, have become proverbial in Iran:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00330
“If the outpouring of the Holy Spirit once again lends its help, others in their turn will do what Christ himself once did.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00331

We must carry the analysis of these differences further. The Plotinian vision, experienced anew by Sohrawardî, is an ecstasy of triumphant joy and exultation. It is an entrance into the Spheres or Heavens of light (aflâk nûrânîya), an admission into a world among beings whose radiance is untouched by anything that might tarnish it in the lower world.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00332

Mîr Dâmâd’s ecstasy, by contrast, reaches its climax in an overwhelming sorrow, brought about by seeing and hearing a distress that embraces the whole of existence. This is precisely what his meditation and his deliberately chosen dhikr had prepared him to encounter. It is as though the invocation becomes contagious throughout the cosmos.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00333

No longer is Mîr Dâmâd alone in reciting it: every universe, and every being within every universe, joins in an immense symphony. Or rather, the visionary himself becomes their organ, their instrument, vibrating with their cry until he can bear no more and loses consciousness. What perceives this sound is not the physical senses, which are adapted to objects outside us, but the Active Imagination alone.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00334

Only this faculty can make such an immaterial resonance present to itself and perceive it: the “immense hidden clamor” that carries its distress from the deepest abyss to the highest reaches of the mystery of being. What this heartrending appeal lays bare is the very secret of the origin of beings, as described by Avicennian cosmology.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00335

But what had been a theoretical description has now burst open into an infinite drama. Its sudden revelation engulfs the mystic and tears him away from the familiar dwelling of his ordinary self. The cosmological pattern in question is well known. It is not a system that establishes the contingency of the world, any more than it establishes the world’s intrinsic necessity, still less anything resembling a supposed “historical necessity.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00336

Rather, it keeps every existing thing suspended between two conditions. On the one hand, each thing necessarily exists through another. Its existence is necessary, certainly, but the source of that necessity lies outside itself.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00337

On the other hand, each thing is incapable of existing through itself. If we imagine its possibility of existing in isolation, that possibility cannot bring itself into being or maintain itself there.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00338

Considered in themselves, beings are merely possible. If they actually exist, then their existence is necessary—but only because they stand in relation to the Being that necessarily gives them existence. This is the Being whose overflowing fullness is sufficient unto itself (al-Ghanî), the Being that makes up for the deficiency of every creature, overcomes its neediness, and grants it what it needs in order to exist through Him (al-Moghnî).
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00339
Now try to grasp, not merely as an idea but as something real, the immense distance between these theoretical considerations and the experience out of which the invocation arises:
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00340
“O You who are sufficient unto Yourself! You who make up for all that is lacking! You who make all things sufficient!”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00341

Then we can begin to measure the distance between a purely theoretical Avicennism and an Avicennism experienced in the depths of the soul, all the way to ecstasy. The two are not simply stages along the same continuous path. There is a break between them, a passage to another level of experience.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00342

A being capable of existing but unable, through itself, to realize that possibility; a being whose necessity comes from Another; in short, an incapacity to create the necessity of one’s own existence, to make up for one’s own nothingness, to possess in oneself what is needed in order to be—this condition is felt from the very summit of existence to its lowest depths, from the angelic world to the realm of inanimate creatures. Mîr Dâmâd’s vision embraced every world, including all the peoples of human history.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00343

From the beginning, each of the cherubic Intelligences of the spiritual pleroma produces the Intelligence that follows it, together with that Intelligence’s own heaven and the Soul that moves that heaven. It does so through a threefold ecstasy. Each of these ecstasies corresponds to one of the three dimensions of its being. The highest dimension is precisely its knowledge that it exists necessarily through the Being that eternally brings it forth.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00344

Yet from the very beginning, in the first of all the Intelligences, there also appears the beginning of a shadow. This belongs to the Intelligence’s lowest dimension: its existence considered as pure possibility. The shadow will grow as the procession descends, until it reaches our earthly world, the “farthest West,” as Avicenna calls it in his Tale of Hayy ibn Yaqzân.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00345

There is a tragedy of being that deepens with every descent from heaven to heaven through the Avicennian cosmos. How could this be reduced to a harmless theoretical diagram, when it gives rise to a spiritual situation whose resolution Avicenna himself had already begun to sketch in his Tale of the Bird? Here, where Mîr Dâmâd has led us to speak specifically of Shiite Avicennism, that resolution begins to appear with distinctive features of its own.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00346

We can discern them not merely as an abstract structure revealed by our analysis, but in the light of what two of Mîr Dâmâd’s closest disciples themselves teach us: Sayyed Ahmad 'Alawî and Qotboddîn Ashkevarî. It is deeply significant that Sayyed Ahmad, when commenting on Avicennian angelology—the doctrine explaining how the Intelligences proceed from one another—explicitly referred to ancient Iranian Zurvanism.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00347

He did so to illuminate the seemingly inevitable appearance of the dimension of Shadow, which arises together with the appearance of the very first Archangel of the pleroma. That Shadow spreads down into our earthly world, accompanied by a growing and boundless distress. This is the distress expressed in the “immense hidden clamor” perceived by Mîr Dâmâd during the hours preceding the night of mid-Sha'bân.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00348

As we have recalled, this is the Night on which the Twelfth Imam was born: the Imam who, since the Greater Occultation (ghaybat), has remained the hidden Imam of this age, the invisible Guide and the Awaited One. The date thus gives its full significance to an explicit connection made by Ashkevarî in a text that deserves to be remembered. For his comparison supplies the necessary complement—the Shiite answer—to the connection that Sayyed Ahmad had established from another direction.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00349

In his lengthy chapter on Zoroaster, or Zarathustra, Ashkevarî mentions the Zoroastrian belief in the Saoshyant, the final Savior who will bring about the “transfiguration” of the world. He does not hesitate to draw a correspondence between the Zoroastrian Saoshyant and the Shiite Twelfth Imam, going so far as to make Zoroaster a prophet who foretells the Imam’s future appearance.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00350

Sayyed Ahmad, for his part, was following the tradition of Sohrawardî’s Eastern or Illuminationist wisdom, Ishrâq, when he turned to the philosophy of ancient Iran. The parallels he discovered between the figures of Zurvanite cosmology and those of Avicennian cosmology were enough to reveal the hidden drama within the latter.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00351

But this drama of the Avicennian cosmos also called for a resolution. The sense that such a resolution must exist is what connects Sayyed Ahmad’s Avicennism, with its Zurvanite coloring, to Ashkevarî’s identification of the ancient Iranian vision of the end of time with the Shiite vision of the same final fulfillment.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00352

And all this occurred long before Western Orientalists began to notice the correspondences between the two. Our Avicennian thinkers made the transition from the concluding pages of Avicenna’s Shifâ' to the opening of Sohrawardî’s Hikmat al-Ishrâq through the idea of the Imam as the “Perfect Human Being.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00353

In the same way, they found the passage from the deliberately Iranian orientation of Ishrâq to Shiite teaching about the Imam by identifying the Saoshyant with the Twelfth Imam. Certainly, the Avicennian cosmology as they understood it equipped them to grasp the meaning of the eternal Ahriman, still undefeated. What we have sketched here is necessarily no more than a brief outline.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00354

Yet it shows one way in which the remarkable and original synthesis of Shiite, Sohrawardian Avicennism took shape: the worldview shared by certain members of the School of Isfahan who were among Mîr Dâmâd’s most distinguished pupils.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00355

Let us now bring this vision together with the personal demand that ta'wîl, spiritual interpretation, makes upon the philosopher-mystic—a demand of which we have already seen an example. Once we do so, it becomes impossible to confine our interpretation of Avicennism within limits that the Iranian Avicennians of Isfahan themselves would certainly never have recognized.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00356

Mîr Dâmâd has given us a personal, experiential confirmation of the ta'wîl he embraces, by recognizing the “Agent Intellect”—the active Intelligence—as the Holy Spirit, the Angel of the Annunciation. In doing so, he reached one of the summits of mystical experience. For here lies the mystery of the soul’s rebirth, the condition of its eternity—a truth of which no theoretical demonstration could ever fully convince the soul.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00357
“But the beings do not know it. The beings are not conscious of it.”
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00358

Hence their “immense hidden clamor.” This was the great lament at the heart of the ecstatic account, the cause of the overwhelming sorrow that brought the visionary almost to unconsciousness. And yet, when he comes back to himself, he is left longing for the very vision that caused such pain.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00359

Are we to say that he longs for that sorrow, that he regrets its passing? Or should we rather say that, within the sorrow and through it, he discovered a sweetness so powerful that it overcame the very cause of his grief? We believe the answer lies in Mîr Dâmâd’s deeply tested Shiite devotion itself. It preserves a paradox that I have already been inclined to describe by placing it alongside one of the paradoxes of Lutheran spirituality: desperatio fiducialis, a despair that nevertheless trusts. Perhaps this is one of the enduring characteristics of Iranian spirituality, reaching back into the distant past: the simultaneous presence of opposites.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00360

We can still experience it in the symphonic poems through which this spirituality expresses itself today, adopting the forms and laws of our own musical language. There is sadness within joy, and joy within sadness. Perhaps this, too, is part of the secret of the Night that marks the birth of the Twelfth Imam.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00361

At the beginning of this chapter, we expressed the hope that, with Mîr Dâmâd as our guide, we might penetrate to the heart of the spiritual city of Isfahan. Perhaps we are now better able to sense the approach to that heart. And, as we suspected from the outset, to sense what this approach means is also to begin to grasp the very secret of a spiritual tradition that remained unknown to us for far too long.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00362

We can now see how Avicennism and Shiism come together. Avicennism has undergone an inner transformation: from a philosophical system explaining the world, it has become a teaching about spiritual life, a form of experience actually lived. It is precisely this dimension of Avicennism that, in the West, people have sometimes found so difficult to understand.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00363

Yet the process itself is not difficult to analyze. One figure dominates Avicenna’s entire account of how knowledge is possible: the Active Intelligence, the Nous poïetikos of the Aristotelians. Unlike the Active Intellect of classical Greek Aristotelianism, however, the Active Intelligence in al-Fârâbî and Avicenna is a separate Intelligence, an angelic Spirit.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00364

Within the hierarchy of angels, it is the Intelligence closest to us, the “Angel of our humanity,” as Sohrawardî calls it (above, Book II, Chapter III). As we have recalled, our philosophers identified this Intelligence with the Holy Spirit, which Quranic revelation in turn identifies with the Archangel of Revelation and the Annunciation. We have repeatedly emphasized the profound implications of this identification.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00365

When the Active Intelligence, which is the Holy Spirit, impresses the forms of knowledge upon the human soul, it is the Holy Spirit thinking itself within that soul and bringing forth there a form of itself. In this way it raises the human intellect from potentiality into actuality—from the capacity to know to the living exercise of knowledge.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00366

Here we begin to discern the idea of the spiritual child (walad ma'nawî): the new being, the true being, gradually brought to birth through our efforts toward an ever-rising horizon of knowledge and love. We have already seen Mîr Dâmâd express this idea in an admirable text, where he presents the mystical experience through the figure of Maryam at the Annunciation.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00367

Perhaps we can now understand more clearly the place occupied by Fâtima in the mandala that took shape in the mind of our master of theology during his vision in the mosque at Qom. We have also glimpsed certain unsuspected correspondences with the spiritual traditions of the West. What Mîr Dâmâd is seeking to express here, Meister Eckhart and Angelus Silesius, each in his own way, have articulated with an unsurpassed depth.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00368

And since we are speaking of the transformation of Avicenna’s doctrine of knowledge into a teaching about spiritual life, we should recall an important fact. In the West, despite the failure of what has been called “Latin Avicennism,” meditation upon this same figure, the Active Intelligence, led Dante’s companions to recognize in it the features of heavenly Wisdom, or Sophia. It was to this figure that they eventually gave the name Madonna Intelligenza—Lady Intelligence.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00369

The admirable text of Mîr Dâmâd does not contain a secret belonging to him alone. That secret gives shape to the entire spiritual tradition whose traces we have been following. The way Mîr Dâmâd meditates upon the Annunciation is exactly the way Mawlânâ Jalâloddîn Rûmî develops it in one of the most beautiful passages of his Mathnawî. It is quite possible that the master of Isfahan remembered Rumi’s account.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00370

Maryam becomes the archetype of mystical experience. After a long period of preparation, the mystic suddenly encounters a person who is at once their own Self and a Self who stands before them as Another. The first impulse is fear and flight.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00371

Only afterward does the mystic recognize that the very presence from which they wish to flee is their Refuge. It is the birth of a new being within the human being. The divine dimension of the person comes into flower: the transcendent heavenly Self, the person’s own true being, but encountered in the “second person,” as a Thou.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00372

This brings us back, finally, to the Mazdean idea of the Fravarti, and to the many variations upon the same theme: the “Perfect Nature” of the Illuminationists (Ishrâqiyûn) (above, Book II, Chapters III and VI); the “invisible guide”; and the “Gabriel of your being” in Semnânî (Book IV, Chapter IV), among others. It is therefore fitting to quote here this magnificent passage from Mawlânâ Rumi’s Mathnawî: At the appearance of a beauty beyond all human measure, Before that Form rising from the earth, blooming like a rose before her, Like an Image lifting its head from the hidden depths of the heart, Maryam, beside herself, seeks refuge in God's protection.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00373

But the Angel says to her: You flee from my visible Form into the invisible... Yet it is in that invisible world that I make my home and dwelling. O Maryam, look carefully, for I am a Form not easily seen.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00374

I am the new Moon, and I am the Image within the heart. When an Image enters your heart and makes its home there, You may flee as far as you wish: that Image will remain within you, Unless it is an empty Image, without substance, Sinking away and disappearing like a false dawn.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00375

But I am like the true dawn. I am the light of your Lord. For no night wanders about my Day... You seek refuge in God against me, Yet from all eternity I am the Image of the one Refuge. I am the refuge that has so often been your deliverance. You seek refuge against me, And I am the Refuge. One hesitates to weaken the suggestive power of this beautiful passage by adding commentary. In any case, a few words could never explain it. It would take an entire book.
I. The Ecstatic Confessions of Mîr Dâmâd
passage-en-00376

Yet in the end, that book could only be the book of our own life—the book each of us is responsible for writing, and which is nothing other than our life itself. For the teaching of Mîr Dâmâd, like that of Sohrawardî, is that the personal search for philosophical understanding and the growth of our spiritual individuality depend upon one another. Neither can reach its fulfillment without the other.

1. The Life and Work of Mollâ Sadrâ
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00379

Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî, the most famous student of Mîr Dâmâd, has appeared so often in the course of this book that it seems almost unnecessary to introduce him here as one of the great figures of Islamic thought—of Shiite thought in particular, and, more particularly still, of the thought and spiritual life of Iranian Islam. Sadroddîn Mohammad ibn Ibrâhim Shîrâzî, more commonly known by his honorific name Mollâ Sadrâ, or as Sadr al-Mota'allihîn (“the foremost of the mystical theosophers”), was born in Shîrâz around 979–980 AH, or 1571–1572 CE, during the reign of Shah Tahmasp (1524–1576).
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00380

We owe this more precise dating to the distinguished Shaykh Mohammad Hosayn Tabâtabâ'î, a professor at the theological university of Qomm. While preparing a new edition of Mollâ Sadrâ's principal work, he discovered a manuscript copied in 1197/1703 from the author's autograph, now lost. It reproduced a number of marginal notes that Mollâ Sadrâ had added to his own text.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00381

Beside the chapter affirming the union (ittihâd) of the knowing subject ('âqil) with the form it knows (ma'qûl), Mollâ Sadrâ had written: “This inspiration came to me at sunrise on Friday, 7 Jomâdâ I, in the year 1037 of the Hijra [14 January 1628], when fifty-eight years of my life had already passed.” The calculation is straightforward: counting back in lunar years places his birth in 979 or 980 AH, corresponding to 1571 or 1572 CE. This date and that of his departure from this world (1050/1640) are the only two dates in his biography of which we can be entirely certain.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00382

But the richness of his life lay elsewhere than in its outward circumstances. Those circumstances chiefly mattered for the difficulties they imposed on him, not because they eased his way toward worldly honors. The true biography of Mollâ Sadrâ is the unfolding of his inner life: the progress of his meditations, the books he wrote, his teaching, and his relationships with students who went on to produce works of which their master could have been proud.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00383

These dates mean that the lunar year 1380 AH (spanning 1960–1961 in our calendar, and corresponding to 1338–1339 in the solar Hijri calendar used in Iran) marked the fourth centenary of our philosopher's birth in Shîrâz. In Iran, the anniversary prompted a number of publications and raised hopes that Mollâ Sadrâ's immense body of work would soon inspire and guide a revival of traditional metaphysics. Those hopes have since found confirmation.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00384

I am thinking particularly of the monumental studies published by our friend Professor Sayyed Jalâloddîn Ashtiyânî, who seems, in some respects, like a Mollâ Sadrâ reborn in our own time. His vast learning, joined to a keen philosophical intelligence, is opening the way to renewed study of traditional philosophy.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00385

There is, on the other hand, a tendency among some writers to interpret Mollâ Sadrâ by making rough comparisons with modern Western philosophies whose basic assumptions are entirely foreign to his thought. Such comparisons disregard the conditions that any serious attempt at comparative philosophy must meet.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00386

For my part, I have tried to contribute as much as I could to this renewal of Islamic philosophical studies, especially in a field that had been almost entirely neglected until our own day. Comparisons, however, must rest not on the likeness of isolated terms but on analogous relationships.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00387

Since such analogies can be found within the respective worlds of thought, I have sometimes suggested that Mollâ Sadrâ's genius combines, in a sense, the constructive, synthesizing power of a Saint Thomas Aquinas with the intuitive vision of a mystical theosopher like Jacob Boehme.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00388

Perhaps so surprising a pairing is possible only within the horizon of ishrâq, the philosophy of illumination. And it is precisely within that horizon that we may hope for the renewal of a kind of thinking which, unlike our passing enthusiasms for this or that philosophy as a mere “moment of history,” seeks access to the eternal reality toward which the fitrat—the human being's original, fundamental nature—is always directed.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00389

We can distinguish three periods in Sadroddîn's life. His father, a man of standing and comfortable means, spared no effort in his son's education; the boy, for his part, showed remarkable early promise, both intellectual and moral. At that time Ispahan was not only the political capital of the Safavid monarchy but also the center of Iran's intellectual life.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00390

The numerous colleges mentioned earlier in connection with Mîr Dâmâd were flourishing there, and some can still be visited today. The greatest teachers were gathered in the city, offering instruction across the whole range of knowledge. It was therefore natural that young Sadroddîn should leave his native Shîrâz to complete his studies in Ispahan.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00391

We must not imagine this course of study on the model of our modern universities, where one earns degrees in a handful of years. It occupied an entire period of life—or rather, it assumed that a person would devote a lifetime to the disciplines he hoped to master. It took at least twenty years to become a mojtahed, a scholar qualified to exercise independent judgment in religious law.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00392

In Ispahan, Sadroddîn studied chiefly with three men whose names are celebrated in the history of Iranian thought and spirituality. The first was Shaykh Bahâ'oddîn 'Amilî, commonly called Shaykh-e Bahâ'î (d. 1030/1621).
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00393

From him Sadroddîn learned the traditional Islamic sciences: tafsîr, or Qur'anic interpretation; Shiite hadîth, the transmitted sayings and teachings; religious law; and related disciplines. He continued until he received his ijâzat, the personal authorization by which a teacher licenses a student to teach in turn. Throughout his life, Shaykh Bahâ'î maintained an exceptionally faithful friendship with the master whose life and work we examined in the previous chapter: Magister tertius, Mîr Dâmâd.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00394

As we have seen, Mîr Dâmâd believed, like Sohrawardî, that philosophy is a vain undertaking unless it leads to spiritual realization and mystical experience. It was to Mîr Dâmâd that Mollâ Sadrâ turned as his master and guide in speculative philosophy, and in this respect he proved a worthy disciple. His reverence for his teacher is illustrated by the little story told earlier (p. 25, n. 20): in an impromptu conversation with a stranger, the young Sadrâ did not hesitate to rank his master among the very greatest. That reverence comes through even more clearly in two letters to Mîr Dâmâd concerning philosophical questions, which have fortunately survived.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00395

One opens with a moving expression of gratitude and ends by placing Mîr Dâmâd among the highest company: if the supreme pleroma, the fullness of the intelligible world, contains ten archangelic Intelligences, Mîr Dâmâd deserves to be counted as the eleventh.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00396

Finally, Sadroddîn is said to have been a student of a quite extraordinary figure, Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî. The evidence is less secure here. Biographical collections agree on the connection, but it is strange that Sadrâ himself never mentions it. In any case, we should recall the intense movement of people and ideas between Iran and India at the time, encouraged by Shah Akbar's generous religious reforms. Many Iranian philosophers, especially followers of Sohrawardî's ishrâqî tradition, gathered at the Mughal sovereign's court.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00397

Mîr Abû'l-Qâsim Fendereskî seems to have been closely involved in the translation of Sanskrit texts into Persian. This was a cultural event of the first importance: through these translations, Hindu thought began to speak Persian in the language of Sufism. (Let us remember that Anquetil-Duperron came to know the Upanishads through their Persian version.) The names of these three masters give us, in broad outline, an idea of the education Mollâ Sadrâ received during the first period of his life: his years of apprenticeship.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00398

Now the second period begins. Learning to think for oneself is never simple, anywhere, for anyone. It requires an uncompromising effort, and the farther an independent thinker advances, the more certain he is to provoke the hostility of every kind of conformism—of all those who fail to understand that there can be no “tradition” without continual “rebirth.”
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00399

Mollâ Sadrâ learned this harsh lesson firsthand. A few lines from the introduction to his great Summa reveal something of his suffering: “In earlier days,” he writes, “from the dawn of my youth, I devoted my efforts, as far as I was given the power to do so, to metaphysics (falsafat ilâhîya, divine philosophy).
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00400

“I studied with the ancient Sages, and afterward with more recent philosophers, gathering the fruits of their inspiration and meditation, benefiting from the first fruits of their innermost awareness and their esoteric knowledge (asrâr). I sought to distill everything I read in the books of the Greek philosophers and others, so as to bring each question down to its essence and avoid all unnecessary elaboration [...]. Unfortunately, obstacles frustrated my purpose; day followed day without my being able to bring it to completion [...].
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00401

“When I saw the hostility that anyone wishing to reform the ignorant and uneducated arouses in our day, when I saw the infernal fire of stupidity and error blazing at full strength [...], and when I came up against the incomprehension of people blind to the lights and secrets of wisdom [...], people whose sight has never passed beyond the boundaries of material appearances, whose thought has never risen above the dwellings of darkness and their dust—people who, because of their hostility to knowledge and gnosis, and because they utterly reject the path of philosophy (hikmat) and certainty gained through personal experience (îqân), have no access to the higher knowledge of divine wisdom ('olûm moqaddasa ilâhîya) or the loftier secrets of gnosis, the knowledge which the prophets and Friends of God expressed in symbols and which the philosophers and gnostics ('orafâ) also pointed toward [...]—then this suffocation of intelligence, this freezing of human nature brought about by the hostility of our age, forced me to withdraw to a remote region, to hide myself in obscurity and distress, cut off from my hopes and brokenhearted [...].
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00402

“Following the teaching of the one who is my master and support, the First Imam, forefather of the holy Imams who are witnesses and Friends of God, I began to practice taqîyeh, the discipline of keeping spiritual mysteries concealed. ...”
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00403

What Mollâ Sadrâ experienced in Ispahan was not peculiar to his age, as perhaps he believed. His vocation and determination were to live and teach Shiism in its fullness, including the mystical knowledge drawn from the Imams' own teaching. In this way the philosopher became caught up in the spiritual tragedy underlying the glorious Safavid period: Sufism had become suspect precisely because it had triumphed with the dynasty, while Shiism had to win back its own identity if it was to preserve its gnostic tradition.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00404

The conversation Sadrâ held in a dream with his master Mîr Dâmâd (see p. 20 above) shows that he continued to feel the effects of this tragedy even in the last period of his life. The harassment of the narrow-minded drove the young philosopher away from Ispahan's vigorous intellectual life and into a remote refuge. He chose the small town of Kahak, some thirty kilometers southeast of Qomm.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00405

Leaving Qomm along the road to Ispahan, one turns off after about a league and a half onto a track running eastward across some fifteen kilometers of desert toward a mountain range. There a high valley opens, displaying the contrast so characteristic of the Iranian landscape: the desert's bare stone gradually gives way, as one climbs the valley, to the enchantment of luxuriant greenery.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00406

Kahak is a place of gardens, enchanting in itself. It also has a small mosque, built in the eleventh Islamic century, with an unusual plan, where Mollâ Sadrâ may once have prayed. Two more recent monuments complete the scene: an Imâm-zâdeh, a shrine associated with a descendant of an Imam, of exquisite design (the Imâm-zâdeh Ma'sûmeh), and a romantic-looking fortress built of fragile material.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00407

I retain a vivid picture of all this, for I needed to know the landscape in which Mollâ Sadrâ spent nine or eleven years meditating and writing, himself living in “the exaltation of solitude.” So a few years ago, in November 1962, I went there on pilgrimage with two dear Iranian companions.
II. Mollâ Sadrâ Shîrâzî
passage-en-00408

But to grasp the full mystical geography of this landscape, one must, on the return journey toward Qomm, leave the main road once again and follow another track eastward to Jam-Karân, to the sanctuary of the one who, for more than ten centuries, has himself been the secret history of Shiite consciousness: the Twelfth Imam, the Hidden Imam.
